clinicalPearls: Infantile Refsum disease is the mildest end of the Zellweger spectrum of peroxisome biogenesis disorders, caused by biallelic PEX-gene variants (most commonly PEX1), not by a single isolated enzyme defect.
It must be distinguished from classic adult Refsum disease, which is a single-enzyme peroxisomal disorder (phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase or PEX7) with isolated phytanic-acid accumulation.
The combination of retinitis pigmentosa with progressive visual loss and sensorineural hearing loss should prompt peroxisomal screening.
Hepatic involvement with hepatomegaly, cholestasis and coagulopathy from fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption is characteristic, as is adrenocortical insufficiency.
Developmental delay, hypotonia and failure to thrive are usual, but dysmorphism is milder than in Zellweger syndrome and survival into later childhood or adulthood is possible.

Biochemistry reflects a generalised peroxisomal defect: raised very-long-chain fatty acids, raised phytanic and pristanic acids, elevated pipecolic acid, abnormal bile-acid intermediates and reduced red-cell plasmalogens.
Because multiple peroxisomal pathways fail together, elevation of very-long-chain fatty acids is the key discriminator from classic Refsum disease, where they are normal.
reference.pathophysiology: Peroxisome biogenesis depends on peroxin (PEX) proteins that import matrix enzymes and assemble the organelle. In infantile Refsum disease, hypomorphic partial loss-of-function variants in a PEX gene permit some residual peroxisomal function, giving a milder phenotype than the near-absent function of Zellweger syndrome. The resulting generalised peroxisomal dysfunction impairs beta-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids, which accumulate, alpha-oxidation of phytanic acid, synthesis of ether phospholipids and plasmalogens, bile-acid synthesis and other peroxisomal reactions. Accumulated lipids and deficient plasmalogens injure the retina, cochlea, liver, adrenal cortex and developing nervous system, producing the characteristic multisystem sensory, hepatic and neurodevelopmental picture. Inheritance is autosomal recessive.
additionalDifferentials: Other Zellweger spectrum disorders (Zellweger syndrome, neonatal adrenoleukodystrophy)
Classic adult Refsum disease (PHYH or PEX7) with isolated phytanic-acid elevation
Single-enzyme peroxisomal beta-oxidation defects such as D-bifunctional protein deficiency
Usher syndrome and other causes of combined retinitis pigmentosa and deafness
Congenital disorders of glycosylation and other multisystem metabolic disorders
additionalInvestigations: Plasma very-long-chain fatty acids as the first-line screen (raised)
Plasma pipecolic acid and bile-acid intermediates
PEX-gene molecular genetic testing via a panel or exome sequencing
Liver function, coagulation and adrenal (cortisol) assessment
redFlags: Coagulopathy or bleeding from fat-soluble vitamin deficiency
Adrenal insufficiency with risk of adrenal crisis
Rapid deterioration of vision or hearing
reference.prognosis: The course is milder than Zellweger syndrome, and survival into later childhood or adulthood is possible, but progressive visual and hearing loss, neurological impairment and hepatic and adrenal complications commonly accrue over time.
pitfalls: Confusing infantile Refsum disease with classic adult Refsum disease and testing only phytanic acid, when very-long-chain fatty acids and other markers are also needed
Attributing combined retinitis pigmentosa and deafness to Usher syndrome without peroxisomal screening
Missing treatable complications such as fat-soluble vitamin deficiency and adrenal insufficiency
Assuming a single normal very-long-chain fatty acid result excludes a peroxisomal disorder without extended or repeat profiling
management: Restrict dietary phytanic acid to limit accumulation of the toxic branched-chain fatty acid
Supplement fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K to correct malabsorption and coagulopathy from cholestatic liver disease
Provide replacement glucocorticoids for adrenocortical insufficiency
Support hearing with aids or cochlear implantation and provide low-vision services for progressive retinitis pigmentosa
Manage cholestatic liver disease, monitor coagulation and consider bile-acid therapy where appropriate
Optimise nutrition and provide developmental support for hypotonia and failure to thrive
Surveil visual, auditory, hepatic, adrenal and neurological function over time
Refer to metabolic medicine and offer genetic counselling with family screening given autosomal recessive PEX-gene inheritance
